37a2a047c46d98417bb95faf.excerpt: WordPress 7.1.5 is a security release, and site owners should update immediately. 19 distinct vulnerabilities are tracked by Wordfence, including one Critical and four High-severity issues based on CVSS v3.1. Notable issues include an unauthenticated privilege escalation that could lead to remote code execution, SQL injection, stored cross-site scripting, XML-RPC denial of service, and a multisite Administrator-to-Super-Administrator privilege escalation. Eight vulnerabilities do not require authentication to exploit. However, several have additional prerequisites or require user interaction, so they are not universally exploitable on every WordPress site. WordPress 7.1.5 was released on November 18, 2026, with fixes for a broad group of security issues affecting WordPress Core. The release addresses privilege escalation, cross-site scripting, SQL injection, information disclosure, authorization bypass, cross-site request forgery, and denial of service. WordPress recommends updating immediately. Most sites with automatic background updates enabled will begin receiving the release automatically, but site owners should still confirm that the update completed. Go to Dashboard > Updates and verify that the site is running WordPress 7.1.5 or the corresponding fixed release for its branch . WordPress 7.1.5 fixes several consequential vulnerabilities. According to WordPress, the Template Part block attribute issue is an unauthenticated privilege escalation that could lead to remote code execution. The release also addresses a Critical privilege escalation on multisite, multiple cross-site scripting vulnerabilities, two SQL injection vulnerabilities, information disclosure, authorization bypass, and denial of service. WordPress 7.1.5 at a Glance 19 distinct vulnerabilities 8 unauthenticated 1 / 4 Critical / High by CVSS v3.1 8 cross-site scripting issues Why Wordfence counts 19 vulnerabilities The official WordPress announcement contains 20 security bullets. Two are expressly described as hardening changes rather than vulnerabilities: a correction to JSON media-type matching and removal of an obsolete Imgur embed variation. That leaves 18 vulnerability bullets. One of those bullets, the authorization bypass in admin comment editing, contains two distinct vulnerabilities. One lets an Author move an approved comment to another user’s post; the other lets an Author change a private editorial Note into a public comment. They have different attacker-controlled fields, impacts, and affected version ranges, so Wordfence tracks them separately. The result is 19 vulnerability records and two hardening changes . The Most Significant Vulnerabilities Multisite Administrator to Super Administrator Privilege Escalation WordPress Core 4.3.0 - 7.1.4 - Authenticated (Administrator+) Privilege Escalation to Super Administrator via Customizer Menu Preview 9.1 CVSS Rating 9.1 (Critical) Affected Version(s) Various Patched Versions 4.7.40, 4.8.35, 4.9.36, 5.0.32, 5.1.29, 5.2.31, 5.3.28, 5.4.26, 5.5.25, 5.6.24, 5.7.22, 5.8.20, 5.9.21, 6.0.19, 6.1.17, 6.2.16, 6.3.15, 6.4.15, 6.5.15, 6.6.12, 6.7.12, 6.8.13, 6.9.12, 7.0.9, 7.1.5 Affected Software WordPress [wordpress] Researcher Yuval Miller WordPress Core is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in versions 4.3.0 through 7.1.4. This is due to insufficient domain separation when hashing Customizer navigation-menu preview arguments. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Administrator-level access and above, on multisite installations to take over a Super Administrator account. More Details > The highest-scoring issue, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.1 (Critical) , affects WordPress multisite. According to WordPress, a site-level Administrator can abuse Customizer navigation-menu preview handling to cross the network-administration boundary and take over a Super Administrator account. This issue requires an authenticated site Administrator and a multisite installation. It does not give an unauthenticated visitor Administrator access, and on a standard single-site installation an Administrator already holds the site’s highest ordinary role. WordPress 7.1.5 separates the security context used to validate navigation-menu preview arguments, preventing the cross-context reuse at the center of the vulnerability. Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation via Template Part Block Attributes WordPress Core 5.9.0 - 7.1.4 - Cross-Site Request Forgery to Administrator Account Creation via Template Part Entity Key 8.8 CVSS Rating 8.8 (High) Affected Version(s) Various Patched Versions 5.9.21, 6.0.19, 6.1.17, 6.2.16, 6.3.15, 6.4.15, 6.5.15, 6.6.12, 6.7.12, 6.8.13, 6.9.12, 7.0.9, 7.1.5 Affected Software WordPress [wordpress] Researcher Logan Homolka WordPress Core is vulnerable to client-side cross-site request forgery through an unsafe Template Part entity key in versions 5.9.0 through 7.1.4. An unauthenticated attacker can prepare a crafted site-editor link that, when opened by an Administrator, makes the editor construct a create-user REST request and attach the victim's nonce. In a paired test, this created an attacker-chosen Administrator on 7.1.4 whose credentials worked in a separate login; 7.1.5 issued no user-creation request. The proven path requires an Administrator to open the link, while a low-privilege stored-input path and remote code execution were not demonstrated. More Details > The WordPress announcement describes this issue as an unauthenticated privilege escalation through Template Part block attributes that could lead to remote code execution. The Wordfence Intelligence record classifies the issue as client-side cross-site request forgery leading to Administrator account creation and assigns it a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 (High) . e1501296045c67fd19436c37.title_original: What Is Preemptive MDR? A Guide For Security Leaders
e1501296045c67fd19436c37.excerpt: When an MDR provider contains a compromised endpoint, your team needs to know whether the weakness that enabled the attack exists elsewhere and who is responsible for addressing it. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in. Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses. How does preemptive MDR differ from traditional MDR? Managed detection and response provides security specialists who monitor, investigate, and respond to threats around the clock. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security. Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. When analysts investigate suspicious activity on a server, knowing that it is internet-facing, supports a critical application, and has a vulnerability under active exploitation helps them assess urgency and determine where to look next. In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address. Within a broader preemptive cybersecurity strategy, MDR connects exposure information with the people investigating and responding to threats. The aim is to reduce opportunities for compromise and intervene before an attack causes harm, while retaining the expertise to contain and recover from incidents. How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR helps teams decide which weaknesses require action first. Exposure context also informs targeted hunting and the investigation of suspicious activity. Consider a hypothetical organization running an internet-facing application affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability. The security team needs to establish whether the vulnerable software is present, what the application supports, and whether attackers are exploiting the weakness. Those findings can guide remediation priorities and targeted hunting for signs of compromise. If suspicious activity appears, analysts investigate it with an understanding of the affected system and the potential route an attacker could take through the environment. Depending on the evidence, the response may involve containing a system, examining related accounts, or expanding the investigation to other assets. The organization’s remediation teams also need clear recommendations about the underlying exposure. What the investigation reveals then feeds back into detection rules, hunting priorities, and response procedures. This gives leaders a way to track an identified risk through investigation, action, and outstanding work, with clearer ownership at each stage. What role does AI play in preemptive MDR? Before analysts can assess a potential threat, they often need to retrieve logs, examine user activity, and connect evidence across several systems. AI can accelerate this work by gathering and correlating information for review. Agentic investigation capabilities can perform elements of that process in parallel, test possible explanations, and organize findings. Their usefulness depends on the available data: missing identity activity or asset information can leave gaps in the account of what happened. Rapid7’s approach keeps human expertise central to validation and response decisions. Analysts assess the evidence alongside the organization’s priorities and the consequences of an action, including whether isolating a system could interrupt a critical service. What to look for in a preemptive MDR provider When evaluating a service described as preemptive, ask the provider to show how exposure information changes its work. A redacted investigation should make clear what analysts knew about the affected asset, how that influenced their reasoning, and which actions followed.If an investigation identified a weakness, was it assigned to an owner and addressed? Did the findings change detection coverage or future priorities? Where AI contributed, the provider should explain its role and the oversight applied. Incident response remains part of the requirement. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response alongside exposure-informed defense and AI-assisted investigation, supporting containment, detailed analysis, and threat eradication. Agree on responsibilities before that support is needed. Establish which actions the provider can take, when customer approval is required, and who owns remediation. Those arrangements determine how findings become action, particularly when taking a system offline carries business consequences. Once the service is operating, review progress through specific cases: exposures addressed before exploitation, threats contained, and weaknesses closed after investigation. Ask to see the evidence behind those outcomes and any work still outstanding, so your team can judge where risk has changed and where further attention is needed. Explore Rapid7 MDR to see how exposure-informed defense, AI-assisted investigation, and expert response work together.

2da806e4a6979c42af5e5590.title_original: Spying on Governments with Zero Lines of Malware: A Custom SoftEther Bridge in Webworm’s Toolkit
2da806e4a6979c42af5e5590.excerpt: Introduction For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need. One example of this is shown by the China-aligned APT known as Webworm, which has been known to deploy the open-source SoftEther VPN into the networks of compromised governmental organizations to maintain low-profile, long-term access. After this was publicly documented and defenders could keep an eye out for this tactic, the actor presumably started thinking of ways to make their covert access stealthier. In this post, we share our analysis of what we believe to be a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence. We additionally provide guidance and tooling for detecting its presence on a system and extracting the configuration(s) associated with it. Technical analysis To illustrate how the tool works, we will use the only public sample of this tool we are aware of, which can be found in our IoCs list ( 90e7… ). The sample is a Windows PE32+ file targeting the x64 architecture. Based on cleartext strings and constants in the binary, we identified it as a (modified) build of the SoftEther VPN Bridge executable, specifically version 4.44, build 9807. Similarly, the PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb . As such, the tool doesn’t hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions. The first and most trivial change the threat actor implements is in the PE metadata. Here we learn that the OriginalFileName of this binary is netcapa.exe , and it brands itself as “Network Monitor Software” published by a company named “Network Systems Solutions Inc.“. The only field unchanged against the stock SoftEther executable ( vpnbridge_x64.exe ) is the Version , which reads 4, 44, 0, 9807 . Next, we wanted to identify any functionality added or modified by the threat actor. The SoftEther bridge alone is a powerful tool to maintain remote access to a compromised network, but we wanted to know if perhaps there was a backdoor to give the threat actor direct command execution on the infected host. For that reason we checked out the corresponding tag in the public “SoftEtherVPN_Stable” repository on GitHub and compared it to the decompiled sample. Internal rebranding The rebranding apparent in the exposed metadata extends into internal strings used in debug banners, service names, registry keys, the contents of the server’s HTTP 401 error page, or firewall rule names, where occurrences of “SoftEther VPN” are replaced by “NtMonitor VPN”. However, the renaming is inconsistent; for example, the service name used by the entry point is still SEVPNBRIDGE , and many registry key paths still reference the “SoftEther Project”. Network stealth Stock SoftEther VPN Mayaqua/Network.h defines HTTP endpoints used by the protocol: HTTP_VPN_TARGET "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi" NtMonitor replaces these endpoints with much more innocent-sounding names, in particular: HTTP_VPN_TARGET "/update/alive.cgi" HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 "/update/picture.cgi" A client initiating a connection to a SoftEther VPN server will send a handshake request to HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 along with a "watermark", i.e. a byte pattern proving that the client is speaking the correct VPN protocol. Otherwise, the server answers with a decoy HTTP response. NtMonitor changes the upstream GIF watermark with a custom byte pattern (a truncated PNG file showing the Windows logo), so that stock SoftEther clients and servers cannot handshake with this build, and NtMonitor's own peers cannot be fingerprinted with the well-known stock GIF watermark. Embedded resource archive As the threat actor probably realizes, a SoftEther resource archive named hamcore.se2, which sits next to the executables in the installation directory and is required to be present at runtime, provides a straightforward detection opportunity for unauthorized installations. We think that, for this exact reason, the actor chose to reduce the contents of this archive to a bare minimum, package the archive inside the bridge executable itself (as a PE resource), and implement a custom resource directory walk to load the archive at runtime. As a side effect, this increases the binary’s size by about 1.5 MB compared to the official build. Encrypted configuration Another weak point (for the attacker) in stock SoftEther is that its configuration is stored on disk in plain text in a well-recognizable format. The actor changes its name from vpn_bridge.config to setting.conf and modifies the configuration loader to handle custom-encrypted files that start with the magic bytes RCEN in ASCII. The rest of the encrypted file has a simple format and includes the encryption key. A Python script to decrypt such files with the actor’s custom RC4-like cipher is available on the Rapid7 Intelligence GitHub repository. Attribution and interpretation of findings Beyond the changes described above, we did not identify any additional malware functionality. Clearly, the threat actor prioritizes stealth above raw capability. It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther’s detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it. At the time of our analysis, only one anti-virus vendor detected the sample on VirusTotal, although it has been public since January. This aligns well with the TTPs previously reported for Webworm by ESET, and such attribution is further supported by indicators in decrypted configurations Rapid7 Intelligence has access to. In all of the cases, the VPN is configured to bridge (“cascade”) a remote network into the local one; furthermore, in cases that were not likely deliberate tests, the remote IP address was located inside AS 20473 belon

68746c06a30918805b320e88.title_original: CVE-2026-123890: Critical Authentication Bypass in VMware vCenter
68746c06a30918805b320e88.excerpt: Overview On November 19, 2026, Broadcom published VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0009 , addressing five vulnerabilities in VMware products. The most severe of these, CVE-2026-123890 , is an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel ( CWE-288 ) in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9.8 . A malicious actor with network access to an affected vCenter deployment may exploit CVE-2026-123890 without credentials to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system as the Administrator user. Mandiant privately reported the issue to Broadcom. Also, Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by Chinese state-linked threat actor ARMORY CASTLE as early as September 2026. CVE-2026-123890 is distinct from the vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-59309 that Broadcom addressed earlier in 2026. The vendor FAQ states that all vCenter systems below the versions fixed by VMSA-2026-0009 require the new update, including systems that already received the earlier fix. Broadcom characterizes the vCenter update as an emergency change requiring prompt action. Mitigation guidance Vendor-provided updates are available for CVE-2026-123890. Broadcom lists no workaround, and the patches cannot be applied using vCenter Quick Patch. Organizations should prioritize upgrading vCenter on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for their deployment. VMware Product Affected Version Fixed Version / Patch VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter Server 7.0 Contact Broadcom Support (extended-support customers) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2 8.0 U3m — KB463116 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 8.0 U3m — KB463116 The fixes are cumulative. The vCenter 8.0 U3m and 9.0.2.0200 updates introduce a “Back-in-Time” restriction that blocks upgrades to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1 ; Broadcom advises customers in an active upgrade to review the vendor FAQ and interoperability matrix. Updating vCenter temporarily makes its management interfaces unavailable, but Broadcom states that running virtual machine and container workloads continue to operate. For the latest affected-version and mitigation guidance, please refer to Broadcom's security advisory and supplemental FAQ . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, InsightVM, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-123890 on VMware vCenter Server with an unauthenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the Nov 20, 2026 content release. Updates November 19, 2026 : Initial publication.

2b21c34c97a73e36f287da44.title_original: PHP 원격 코드 실행 가능한 ‘PHPAfterShell’ 취약점(CVE-2026-126714 외 17건) 보안 업데이트 권고
2b21c34c97a73e36f287da44.excerpt: 생성형 AI 제작 이미지 The PHP Group이 11월 19일 PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 보안 릴리스를 공개하고, 원격 코드 실행(RCE)으로 이어질 수 있는 Critical 등급 7건을 포함해 총 18건의 취약점을 수정했습니다. 이번 업데이트에는 지난 10월 긴급 패치된 'PHP2Shell' 취약점 중 CVE-2026-109619의 수정을 보완하는 패치 2건(CVE-2026-129182, CVE-2026-129481)이 포함되어 있습니다. 10월 패치 버전인 PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35도 이번 업데이트 대상이므로, 당시 업데이트를 완료한 환경도 다시 업데이트해야 합니다. PHP 원격 코드 실행 취약점 2종[CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619] 긴급 업데이트 권고 (10/27 취약점 점검 스 The PHP Group이 PHP 엔진 자체에서 발견된 심각한 원격 코드 실행(RCE) 취약점 2건을 긴급 패치했습니다. 'PHP2Shell'로도 불리는 이번 취약점은 웹 애플리케이션 코드가 아닌 PHP 런타임에 존재합니다. blog.alyac.co.kr 특히 'phpAfterShell'로 불리는 CVE-2026-126714는 PHP의 기본 세션 저장 방식인 파일 기반 세션 핸들러에 존재하는 취약점으로, 애플리케이션에 역직렬화 가젯 체인이 있으면 원격 코드 실행으로 이어질 수 있습니다. 이 취약점은 10월 패치 버전에서도 수정되지 않았습니다. PHP 보안팀은 이번 릴리스가 정기 릴리스 주기에 따른 업데이트이며, Critical 등급 취약점은 기본값이 아닌 설정이나 흔치 않은 구성에서 발생한다고 밝혔습니다. 다만 홍콩 침해사고대응팀(HKCERT)이 11월 20일 CVE-2026-126714와 CVE-2026-115560의 개념증명(PoC) 코드가 공개되어 있다고 알린 만큼, 사용자분들의 신속한 업데이트를 권고 드립니다. 보안 업데이트 개요 대상 제품 PHP 8.5 / 8.4 / 8.3 / 8.2 공개일 2026.11.19 수정된 취약점 총 18건 (Critical 7건, High 4건, Moderate 6건, 번들 라이브러리 업데이트 1건) 최고 심각도 Critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2) 주요 영향 원격 코드 실행, 로컬 권한 상승, 서비스 거부(DoS), 정보 노출 PHP2Shell 관련 CVE-2026-109619 보완 패치 2건 포함 (CVE-2026-129182, CVE-2026-129481) 별칭 phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) 조치 PHP 8.5.13 / 8.4.28 / 8.3.37 / 8.2.36 이상으로 업데이트 [표 1] PHP 11월 보안 업데이트 개요 ■ 사용자 권고 사항 운영 서버, 컨테이너 이미지, 개발 환경의 PHP 버전을 확인합니다. 패치 버전(8.5.13 / 8.4.28 / 8.3.37 / 8.2.36) 미만이면 업데이트합니다. 10월 PHP2Shell 권고에 따라 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35로 업데이트한 환경도 다시 업데이트합니다. PHP 8.1 이하 버전은 공식 보안 지원이 종료되었으므로 지원 중인 버전으로 업그레이드합니다. 즉시 업데이트가 어려운 경우 아래 「조치 방법」의 임시 대응 설정을 적용합니다. 36265c91862671070112c65c.title_original: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
36265c91862671070112c65c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

ae3f2217739ca53fc5a5a0eb.title_original: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
ae3f2217739ca53fc5a5a0eb.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

01fc97cca03e91862ebc2217.title_original: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
01fc97cca03e91862ebc2217.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.

8f71b413a3c16df6e44436b3.title_original: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
8f71b413a3c16df6e44436b3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

65a19a85c3a6337574cbcb1b.title_original: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
65a19a85c3a6337574cbcb1b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

76da44ac7bcc0b89d26771d0.title_original: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
76da44ac7bcc0b89d26771d0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.

0b8aafa4d79391f05e87fc80.title_original: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
0b8aafa4d79391f05e87fc80.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.

4b9339b60a9825430cec34cc.title_original: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
4b9339b60a9825430cec34cc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

f5618065c92a5221dee234c1.title_original: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
f5618065c92a5221dee234c1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.

0b7e3816e66f4a1e5f745fc6.title_original: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
0b7e3816e66f4a1e5f745fc6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

ec2230f11bf7519604c95bb3.title_original: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
ec2230f11bf7519604c95bb3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

c009277c2fd0a46a85eb85a0.title_original: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
c009277c2fd0a46a85eb85a0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.

15033fe789f7a9f9e9b8e820.title_original: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
15033fe789f7a9f9e9b8e820.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

77aaf655cff70e084a1ddb0b.title_original: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
77aaf655cff70e084a1ddb0b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

9eb4cd95fe4d3dee2f66cc86.title_original: MS-Point: Multi-Modal Hierarchical Spectral Learning for Point Cloud Understanding
9eb4cd95fe4d3dee2f66cc86.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.

87c35d2ee1c284a76950bd3a.title_original: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
87c35d2ee1c284a76950bd3a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

2a74ab14a165ad25bd1d5efc.title_original: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
2a74ab14a165ad25bd1d5efc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

102c5da87172155a37c4d65f.title_original: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
102c5da87172155a37c4d65f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

031f1fb2f842b9e1b29a5123.title_original: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
031f1fb2f842b9e1b29a5123.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.

07a96b36a154183244b13d65.title_original: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
07a96b36a154183244b13d65.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

eb37871208261623b7bc23fe.title_original: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
eb37871208261623b7bc23fe.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.

b8fafff6a4e6b081fd1011f9.title_original: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
b8fafff6a4e6b081fd1011f9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

48bb201b612819d3e9797a39.title_original: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
48bb201b612819d3e9797a39.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

1c93e7793e75dfc67612718f.title_original: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
1c93e7793e75dfc67612718f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

befe5a2c996bd004c6ee2e61.title_original: When Should a Voice Agent Speak? End-of-Turn Detection in Turkish
befe5a2c996bd004c6ee2e61.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A voice agent that waits for a fixed silence before replying either interrupts users who pause mid-utterance or responds late to users who have finished. This study examines the decision at the onset of silence, using turn ends and turn-internal pauses extracted from the Real-TurnTurk corpus of Turkish dyadic video calls. A fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT model, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a deployed multilingual detector are compared, together with voice-activity timing and facial features, under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation with paired cluster bootstrap tests. On held-out recordings, the fine-tuned model separates turn ends from pauses better than both text baselines and is the best calibrated of the three. Timing features of the current speaker are similarly informative, and their combination with the fine-tuned text score gives the best timing-based results; with logistic regression, this combination also outperforms the same combination with either text baseline. In a latency simulation, adding the text score to a silence timeout shortens the mean response delay at the same interruption rate. On automatic Whisper transcripts, the fine-tuned model retains its advantage over the zero-shot model.

6cab1c44ddf899943d9d8e7b.title_original: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
6cab1c44ddf899943d9d8e7b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.

db742fd8c99d4706398ad809.title_original: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
db742fd8c99d4706398ad809.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.

5e27d062a30c187c49378cb8.title_original: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models
5e27d062a30c187c49378cb8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion and flow models yield a preview, their clean-image estimate, at every denoising step. When they miscount, drop or misplace objects, test-time search is in a bind: its verifiers are reward models built for finished images, so judging early misreads blurry previews, and judging late, as best-of-N does, pays to fully denoise doomed candidates. We find that the image is not the problem: the outcome is settled as denoising starts, by the seed or by a stochastic sampler's first steps, and already shows in early previews; what fails on them is the judge, as reward models read them near chance on several kinds of prompts. We introduce Keystone, a training-free judge of previews that compiles a prompt into typed questions about its objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model answer them. Asked this way, the judge reads counts and positions from early previews better than reward models read them from finished images. Searching at these key steps on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning significantly outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half its generator compute, and as a drop-in verifier there, the Keystone score significantly improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering; without retuning, both searches stay significantly above the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average over four base models and three benchmarks. Keystone thus moves test-time judgment to the key steps where the outcome already shows.

1d6b6ee472a745fa207517fb.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research

4e04b583dd2a84ef13077792.title_original: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
4e04b583dd2a84ef13077792.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.

df3d2a293b6c33cf4b6edfb8.title_original: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
df3d2a293b6c33cf4b6edfb8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice. We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624. COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.

052d02f79ecf416989ebd0e6.title_original: Efficient Multimodal Agents for Auditing 3D Worlds
052d02f79ecf416989ebd0e6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.

25846d3c8675e6a50c2e9c9b.title_original: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
25846d3c8675e6a50c2e9c9b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $\pi(a\mid x,m)$.

b3dfe84a7b711f4ea6b502be.title_original: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
b3dfe84a7b711f4ea6b502be.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.

69fcde611dea4c440f6bd4ad.title_original: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents
69fcde611dea4c440f6bd4ad.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.

b6e2a260d877ca875e8f8cc5.title_original: Learning Networked Dynamical Systems via Neural ODE-based Graph Structure Inference
b6e2a260d877ca875e8f8cc5.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring the latent interaction graph from multivariate time series is fundamental to understanding complex dynamical systems in neuroscience, biology, and physics. Despite recent progress in neural relational inference, most methods rely on discrete-time modeling, which degrades under sparse and irregular observations and tends to entangle multi-hop dependencies into spurious direct edges.
