GPUThor also enables the first Rowhammer exploits on ECC-protected GPUs, inducing uncorrectable double and triple bit flips, making denial-of-service and privilege-escalation attacks practical even on GPUs with ECC enabled.

900841249178d2873a77fc20.title_original: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
900841249178d2873a77fc20.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes an authenticated shared key without giving third parties proof of participation. Post-quantum DAKEs use ring signatures, message authentication codes, or split key-encapsulation mechanisms, which differ in who can authenticate and how deniability is achieved. We introduce \emph{authentication allocation} to classify which parties hold secrets that produce accepted authentication messages. For protocols using a fixed two-member ring, we prove that an accuser can simulate a session by either sharing the accused party's authentication key or signing with its own ring key. Thus, deniability relies on key sharing or the ring signature's ability to hide its signer. We propose \HDKEM, combining ML-KEM-768, X25519, and an optional pre-shared or quantum key distribution (QKD)-delivered key $k_3$ through a split-key pseudorandom function. The session key remains secret if at least one input remains secure. Since provisioning services and QKD key managers may know $k_3$, the client always authenticates with its own ring key; the mode determines whether other holders of $k_3$ can impersonate the server. Four modes are supported: \emph{source-backed} authenticates the server through key confirmation under $k_3$, allowing its holders to impersonate the server; \emph{hide} also encrypts the client's signature; \emph{mutual} adds a server ring signature to prevent such impersonation; and \emph{source-less} authenticates both endpoints with ring signatures without $k_3$. We prove extended Canetti--Krawczyk (eCK) session-key secrecy in the quantum random-oracle model, explicit authentication, forward secrecy, and session-partner deniability, with a concrete deniability bound in the classical random-oracle model. With FalconRS, source-backed mode sends 3,813~bytes in about 26~ms, versus 5,101~bytes and 47~ms in mutual mode.

82e1cc5e704d0735dc67beba.title_original: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
82e1cc5e704d0735dc67beba.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22899v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

409cb565d9a02409139a54c1.title_original: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
409cb565d9a02409139a54c1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22913v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

be66ee298decfcb1fc33dd91.title_original: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
be66ee298decfcb1fc33dd91.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10403v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup. QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

ca79ada1427cd12e23fc5b15.title_original: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
ca79ada1427cd12e23fc5b15.excerpt: arXiv:2602.10510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $\Theta((\varepsilon \beta)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $\beta$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.

dc295e733e2cefbc484e816b.title_original: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
dc295e733e2cefbc484e816b.excerpt: arXiv:2605.19149v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks. We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.

eef424c8d39333af8c3b65c0.title_original: Multidimensional Reconciliation in Continuous-Variable QKD: Review, Coding Schemes, and Open-Source Simulation
eef424c8d39333af8c3b65c0.excerpt: arXiv:2606.02323v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) requires highly efficient reconciliation techniques to operate at low signal-to-noise ratios and long distances. Multidimensional reconciliation addresses this challenge by transforming the physical Gaussian quantum channel into a virtual binary-input additive white Gaussian noise (BIAWGN) channel, enabling the use of modern errorcorrecting codes. In this work, we review the principles of multidimensional reconciliation, with a particular focus on high-dimensional constructions beyond the algebraic dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8. We describe the construction of the virtual channel, discuss practical coding schemes for reverse reconciliation, and analyse their integration with linear error-correcting codes. We also present an opensource simulation framework, HDirac, implementing multidimensional reconciliation for arbitrary dimensions, and use it to evaluate state-of-the-art LDPC codes. The results highlight key trade-offs between dimension, reconciliation efficiency, and frame error rate, providing practical guidance for CV-QKD system design.

80c273ad8ba6acb6e496c09c.title_original: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM
80c273ad8ba6acb6e496c09c.excerpt: We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage. Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate. With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch. Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain. Reimagining security operations for the agentic era On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment. Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security. Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible . Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average . Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster. A shared foundation for people and agents AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most. By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability. Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes. Looking ahead The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread. We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel. Learn more Explore Microsoft Sentinel . Learn about the Integrated Security Operations Center in Microsoft Defender. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website . Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity. CVE-2026-93637 ( #22070 ) Is a rate-limit bypass in Zimbra's Network Edition GraphQL authentication endpoint, which lets credential-stuffing attempts skip the source-IP lockout counter that normally protects the SOAP login path. 618979d3c2e1cfb16b7870b5.excerpt: arXiv:2611.18543v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

da9ef14d67ada93f50013970.title_original: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
da9ef14d67ada93f50013970.excerpt: arXiv:2611.13971v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.

9ecdae5781f925d2b333fb5f.title_original: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
9ecdae5781f925d2b333fb5f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.18372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under four years the field has grown from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. VLA research joins robotics, computer vision and language modelling, so this survey is written for researchers and practitioners from each of these fields. It reviews 89 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. Seven design axes follow a VLA's life cycle: model design (inputs and memory, architecture, action output, intermediate predictions), training (pretraining data, post-training) and deployment (real-time execution). We compare 22 models on these axes, with their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge. (i) Training data has broadened beyond teleoperated robot data (about 10,000 hours for $\pi_0$) to community-collected episodes and egocentric human video (20,000 hours for GR00T N1.7). (ii) Model sizes have split into two groups: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters; a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs. (iii) Generalist VLAs handling both manipulation and navigation are emerging, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions, and review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail after small scene changes. A practitioner's guide gives a default for each design decision, and a glossary supports readers new to the field.

714e572e6a6d9cddd26a5524.title_original: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
714e572e6a6d9cddd26a5524.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22432v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

11321c75a5ffaf1707548a75.title_original: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
11321c75a5ffaf1707548a75.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22897v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

82e645b523188530233b02c7.title_original: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
82e645b523188530233b02c7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

ae472cc4fca6f684960d1215.title_original: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
ae472cc4fca6f684960d1215.excerpt: arXiv:2611.24254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

1b731a994669753de0b25e00.title_original: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
1b731a994669753de0b25e00.excerpt: arXiv:2611.24650v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

d4774f62c4d27cde705714e7.title_original: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
d4774f62c4d27cde705714e7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.24869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

9a3dabcc9aa137a96ac22b5c.excerpt: arXiv:2606.14990v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

06d4951ab066e8d843d8f8f3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09892v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

45e763e0f952c71a75818431.title_original: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
45e763e0f952c71a75818431.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12805v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $\Phi$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

0f18246833086ec94db08e42.title_original: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
0f18246833086ec94db08e42.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22639v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

ad056b969c5c67fd6d02592b.title_original: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
ad056b969c5c67fd6d02592b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23446v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

9197cca535f5e9487e789e42.title_original: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
9197cca535f5e9487e789e42.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled projector rows and noise in the vision encoder, infers the unknown scale factors, and returns most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values and accuracy to near its original level. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry, a cue that a real failure need not leave. When we round those bits away, each model answers our test questions as before, but the agent, unaided, no longer repairs either model: on LFM2-VL accuracy recovers by about 4 points, against 17 from the unrounded weights. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling. On SmolVLM the agent uses it once a sentence in the prompt, which we wrote knowing the fault, names such a statistic; on LFM2-VL, whose scale factors are larger, most sessions find the rescaled rows unaided, but none finds the noise. Swapped rows or columns, which keep the set of stored values, are not found unaided on either model within our budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.

582907dc752bc8447658057b.title_original: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
582907dc752bc8447658057b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence. We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising. Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

05729448dd07c8a368832a47.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23350v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

cd0250d395167a1990b36e71.title_original: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices
cd0250d395167a1990b36e71.excerpt: arXiv:2611.24133v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.

2568382938969809792e2533.title_original: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
2568382938969809792e2533.excerpt: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. ab946592bf354e8fe90b8459.title_original: CVE-2026-129289 and Other Critical PHP Vulnerabilities: What WordPress Site Owners Need to Know
ab946592bf354e8fe90b8459.excerpt: PHP published advisories for several critical vulnerabilities on November 19, 2026, with fixed PHP releases published on November 18 and 19. WordPress site owners should update PHP as soon as possible. CVE-2026-129289 is the most directly relevant issue for WordPress. On an affected PHP-FPM server, an unauthenticated attacker may be able to make PHP run a request that never passed through the web server’s normal checks. Not every WordPress site is exposed. The demonstrated attack requires a vulnerable PHP version and a web server that reuses its private connections to PHP-FPM. Standard NGINX configurations do not enable that reuse by default. The Wordfence Threat Response team confirmed unauthenticated code execution in an isolated WordPress lab. The same test did not run code after PHP was updated or after reuse of the web-server-to-PHP connection was disabled. Fixed releases for the affected supported branches are 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. Hosting vendors may also provide backported fixes under different package version numbers. On November 19, 2026, PHP published CVE-2026-129289 , a critical PHP-FPM vulnerability with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10 . Successful exploitation can let an attacker run PHP code with the permissions of the website’s PHP process. This is a vulnerability in PHP, not WordPress Core, a plugin, or a theme. However, normal WordPress REST API processing provides one of the application behaviors needed by the attack. Updating WordPress will not update PHP. On managed hosting, follow guidance from your host. On a self-managed server, install the PHP fix and restart or redeploy the affected service. How CVE-2026-129289 Works A web server such as NGINX normally checks an incoming request and then passes it to PHP-FPM over a private connection. CVE-2026-129289 can cause PHP to leave part of a request unread. If the web server keeps that private connection open and reuses it, PHP may treat the leftover bytes as a new request. That second request did not go through the web server’s normal routing or access checks. According to PHP’s advisory, an attacker who knows the path to an existing PHP file can use it to run PHP code without logging in. The attack does not depend on corrupting memory, predicting a memory address, or winning a timing race. The required connection reuse is not NGINX’s default. NGINX documents fastcgi_keep_conn off as the default . However, this is a real production setting: WordOps, a server-management tool for WordPress, currently enables fastcgi_keep_conn on and defines cached PHP-FPM connections in its NGINX templates. PHP’s advisory also identifies Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on as an affected configuration. Our lab testing covered NGINX, not Apache. Why WordPress Is Relevant PHP’s advisory says the application must open php://input , which represents the incoming request body, while affected bytes remain unread. WordPress REST requests normally call WP_REST_Server::serve_request() , which uses WP_REST_Server::get_raw_data() to read php://input . In our tested path, a specially formed request body made PHP’s parser stop early, and the PHP bug left crafted bytes on the reused private connection when WordPress reached this code. This REST request behavior is part of stock WordPress Core. The demonstrated route did not require a vulnerable plugin or theme, a WordPress account, an existing session, or attacker-created content. The server still had to be running a vulnerable PHP-FPM release and reusing the private connection between the web server and PHP. What Wordfence Testing Found The Wordfence Threat Response team reproduced unauthenticated PHP code execution through a stock WordPress 7.1.5 REST request in an isolated lab. The vulnerable target used PHP 8.2.35 behind NGINX with PHP-FPM connection reuse enabled. The same request did not run code on an otherwise matched PHP 8.2.36 target or when connection reuse was disabled. As of November 20, 2026, CVE-2026-129289 is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Public technical details are available, so site owners should not wait for evidence of exploitation before updating. Affected and Fixed PHP Versions Affected PHP versions First fixed PHP release PHP 5.6.0 through 8.1.x (unsupported branches) No fixed release; move to a supported branch PHP 8.2.0 through 8.2.35 8.2.36 PHP 8.3.0 through 8.3.36 8.3.37 PHP 8.4.0 through 8.4.27 8.4.28 PHP 8.5.0 through 8.5.12 8.5.13 PHP says the vulnerable code dates to PHP 5.6.0, so unsupported PHP 5.6 through 8.1 releases may also be affected. Sites on unsupported branches should move to a supported, fixed release. Linux distributions and hosting vendors may backport the fix without changing the first three version numbers. If your host manages PHP, check its security notices, status page, dashboard, or customer communications for guidance. If you manage the server, check the complete package revision and the vendor’s security notice. Also make sure you are checking the PHP-FPM version that serves the website; the command-line PHP version can be different. summary.summary_ko: AG-UI는 에이전트와 사용자 간 상호작용을 위한 프로토콜이다. 에이전트를 프런트엔드 애플리케이션에 통합하도록 지원하는 프로젝트다.

summary.title_ko: Claude-BugHunter, 버그 탐색·외부 레드팀 작업용 Claude Code 스킬 모음
summary.summary_ko: Claude Code에서 버그 탐색과 외부 레드팀 작업에 활용하도록 구성된 스킬 묶음이다. 저장소 설명에 따르면 스킬 82개와 슬래시 명령 15개, 핵심 취약점 24개 분류에서 선별한 공개 보고서 패턴 681개를 담았으며, 기업용 신원 체계와 인프라 공격 매트릭스도 포함한다.

summary.title_ko: google-labs-code/stitch-skills, Stitch MCP 연동용 에이전트 스킬 모음
summary.summary_ko: Stitch MCP 서버와 연동하도록 설계된 Agent Skills 라이브러리다. 각 스킬은 Agent Skills 공개 표준을 따라 Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor 같은 코딩 에이전트와의 호환을 지원한다.
summary.background_ko: 여러 코딩 에이전트와의 호환성을 확보하기 위해 각 스킬이 Agent Skills 공개 표준을 따르도록 설계됐다.

summary.title_ko: NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator, AI 에이전트 스킬·플러그인 평가 프레임워크
summary.summary_ko: NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator는 AI 에이전트의 스킬과 플러그인을 여러 단계로 평가하는 프레임워크다. 품질 기준 검사, 의미적 중복 탐지, 합성 평가 데이터 생성과 함께 스킬이 에이전트 동작에 미치는 영향을 측정하는 실제 에이전트 평가 기능을 제공한다.

summary.title_ko: ffmpeg-skill, 코딩 에이전트용 로컬 영상 편집 도구 공개
summary.summary_ko: ffmpeg-skill은 Claude Code, Cursor, Codex에서 사용할 수 있는 로컬 영상 편집 저장소로, FFmpeg 도구 42개와 기계 판독형 규약, MCP 서버를 제공한다. 영상 자르기, 자막, 화면 재구성, 음량 조정과 플랫폼별 내보내기를 지원하며 클라우드나 API 키가 필요 없다고 소개한다.

summary.title_ko: PaperOrchestra, 다중 에이전트 기반 AI 연구 논문 작성 자동화 프레임워크
summary.summary_ko: PaperOrchestra는 AI 연구 논문 작성을 자동화하는 프레임워크다. 여러 에이전트를 활용하는 구조로, 저장소 이름은 google-research/paper-orchestra다.

summary.title_ko: last30days-skill, 여러 온라인 출처를 조사·요약하는 AI 에이전트 스킬
summary.summary_ko: last30days-skill은 Reddit, X, YouTube, HN, Polymarket과 웹에서 주제를 조사하는 AI 에이전트용 스킬이다. 저장소 설명에 따르면 조사한 내용을 종합해 근거에 기반한 요약을 만든다.

summary.title_ko: Arcane, 폭넓은 사용자를 위한 Docker 관리 도구
summary.summary_ko: Arcane은 Docker 관리를 위한 도구다. 누구나 사용할 수 있도록 설계된 현대적인 관리 환경을 표방한다.
모두를 위한 웹 개발을 표방하는 sveltejs/svelte GitHub 저장소다.

summary.title_ko: affaan-m/ECC, 코딩 에이전트 실행 환경 성능 최적화 시스템
summary.summary_ko: ECC는 Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor 등을 위한 에이전트 실행 환경 성능 최적화 시스템이다. 스킬, 행동 패턴, 메모리, 보안과 사전 조사 중심 개발을 다룬다.

summary.title_ko: obra/superpowers, 에이전트 스킬 프레임워크와 개발 방법론
summary.summary_ko: obra/superpowers는 에이전트용 스킬 프레임워크를 제공하는 저장소다. 소프트웨어 개발 방법론도 함께 제시한다.

summary.title_ko: Cursor 플러그인 명세와 공식 플러그인 저장소
summary.summary_ko: Cursor의 플러그인 명세를 담은 저장소다. 공식 플러그인도 함께 제공한다.

summary.title_ko: minimind, 6,400만 매개변수 LLM을 처음부터 학습하는 프로젝트
summary.summary_ko: 6,400만 개 매개변수의 대규모 언어모델(LLM)을 처음부터 학습하는 프로젝트다. 저장소 설명은 이를 2시간 만에 학습할 수 있다고 소개한다.
